title: Who Can Do What?
summary: Read permissions with ls -l, change them with chmod and run a script with ./ (dot slash).
intro:
Every file has a little lock with three keys: read, write and run.
The computer checks these keys before it lets anyone open, change or start a file.
In this lesson you will read the locks, make your diary private, and turn a plain text file into a program you can run.
outro: Now you know who can do what! ls -l shows the locks, chmod changes them, and ./ runs a program from the folder you are in. Remember: 600 for secrets, 644 for normal files, 755 for scripts. And never 777.

steps.instruction: Show the files in this folder in the long format, so you can see their permissions.
hints: Use ls with the option -l. The l means 'long'.
steps.explain: Look at the start of each line: -rw-r--r--. The first - means 'a normal file' (d would mean a folder). Then come three groups of three letters: the owner (you), the group, and everybody else. r = read, w = write, x = execute (run), and - = not allowed.

steps.instruction: Right now everybody can read your diary. Oops! Make diary.txt private: only you can read and write it. Set its mode to 600.
hints: chmod changes the mode. Numbers: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Add them up: 6 = 4 + 2 = read + write. 0 = nothing at all.
steps.explain: The three digits are for owner, group and others. 600 means rw------- : you can read and write, nobody else can do anything. Run ls -l again if you want to see the change.

steps.instruction: hello.sh is a tiny script. Try to run it with ./hello.sh (it will fail, and that's the point!)
hints: ./ means 'the file right here in this folder'.
steps.explain: Permission denied! hello.sh has no x (execute) permission, so the computer refuses to run it. This protects you: a file can't start just because it is there.

steps.instruction: Make hello.sh runnable: give it the mode 755.
steps.explain: 755 means rwxr-xr-x : you can do everything, the others can read and run it, but not change it. This is the normal mode for scripts and programs. You will also see chmod +x hello.sh, which just adds the x.

hints: Same command as before. Use the up arrow key to get it back!
steps.explain: You just ran a program from a file! One warning from Ank: never use chmod 777. It lets EVERYONE change your file, and that is how bad things sneak in.
